# Supply Chain Resilience & Responsible Sourcing — First Draft

**Circulated for comment, not for decision.** Prepared for the Managing Director, with Procurement, Operations, Quality, Engineering, Legal/Compliance and Finance in attendance. Figures marked *illustrative* are placeholders pending the 90-day diagnostic; the architecture, ownership and decision requests are not placeholders.

---

## 0. Executive summary

**The situation, without attribution of fault.** We buy from a supplier base assembled over many years, largely on landed cost and quality performance — which were, at the time, the right criteria. Recent events have made visible a second and third set of criteria that were always present but rarely priced: *how quickly can this source be replaced*, and *what is happening two tiers behind it that we cannot currently see*. Both questions are now being asked of us by customers, by insurers, by lenders, and — increasingly, and with legal force — by regulators in the jurisdictions we sell into.

**The two agendas are usually presented as a trade-off. We would suggest they are largely the same programme.** The same blind spot — no visibility below tier 1 — produces both the sudden allocation shock and the unauthorised subcontracting to an unaudited site. The same commercial reflex — squeeze price, compress lead time, change the order late — produces both the financially fragile supplier and the excessive-overtime finding. A programme that treats resilience and ethics as one visibility-and-relationship problem will cost materially less than two programmes that treat them as separate compliance functions.

**The organising principle we would put forward:**

> *We do not buy parts. We buy the continued ability of a specific site, with specific people, to make them.*
>
> Everything that follows is an attempt to make that ability **visible**, **replaceable**, and **worth preserving** — in that order.

**What we would ask colleagues to consider committing to, in three deliberate stages:**

| | Commitment | Earned by | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stage 1** | Every Tier-1 supplier mapped; every **single point of failure** named and owned; a working ethical risk-screen across 100% of direct spend | Diagnostic + existing data, near-zero capital | Day 90 |
| **Stage 2** | **Time-to-Survive exceeds Time-to-Recover** for all Class A parts; worker-voice coverage at every high-risk site | Dual-qualification, positioned buffers, grievance channels | Month 12 |
| **Stage 3** | Sub-tier traceability to the point of legal defensibility (UFLPA, CSDDD, EUDR as applicable); disruption drills passed, not merely run | Multi-tier mapping, chain-of-custody, supplier development | Month 24–36 |

**Illustrative investment (order of magnitude; to be firmed at Day 90):**

| Item | Year-1 cost | Working capital | Note |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Multi-tier mapping & risk-sensing platform (subscription) | £0.12–0.25M/yr | — | Buy, don't build; 8–12 weeks to useful output |
| Dual-qualification programme (~30–50 Class A parts) | £0.35–0.60M | — | Tooling, PPAP/FAI, sample runs; the largest single line |
| Strategic buffer inventory, positioned by TTS gap | — | £1.5–2.5M | Deliberately *not* uniform; see §5.3 |
| Capacity reservation / option fees | £0.10–0.20M/yr | — | Cheaper than inventory for long-lead, low-value items |
| Ethical due diligence: screening, audits, worker-voice tooling | £0.20–0.35M/yr | — | Worker-voice is ~15% of the cost of audit and finds more |
| Supplier development fund (co-investment, not charity) | £0.15–0.30M/yr | — | Ring-fenced, merit-allocated |
| Supply chain finance facility (early-payment for SMEs) | ~£0.05M setup | (off-balance-sheet) | Improves supplier solvency *and* removes a root cause of labour abuse |
| Programme resource (lead + analyst) | £0.22M/yr | — | Two people. Not a department |
| **Total** | **£1.2–2.0M** | **£1.5–2.5M** | |

**Illustrative return.** On assumptions to be validated by Day 60: avoided disruption cost of *£1.5–3.0M/yr* (expedited freight, premium spot buys, line stoppages, late-delivery penalties, lost orders), plus tender eligibility we currently forfeit — several of our larger customers now screen on documented due diligence, and we would want to size that before quoting it. Regulatory exposure avoided is real but should be presented as *insurance, not return*. Indicative payback **18–30 months**. *If the Day-60 disruption-cost reconstruction does not support the figure, the correct recommendation is to fund the mapping and the near-zero-cost workstreams and stop there — those alone are defensible.*

**Decisions requested (also §13):** appoint sponsor and Supply Resilience Lead (Week 0); authorise the diagnostic and the risk-sensing subscription (Week 0); approve the revised supplier scorecard and the internal purchasing-practices review (Week 6); approve capital, working capital and the supplier code refresh (Day 90).

---

## 1. How we would suggest this is taken forward

This is a plan that fails quietly if it is simply approved and delegated. Before anything is presented collectively, we would propose:

1. **Separate conversations with each function first.** Procurement will hear "resilience" as a challenge to buying decisions they made under the criteria they were given. Operations will hear "buffer inventory" as a working-capital fight they have previously lost. Sales will hear "responsible sourcing" as a cost that arrives before the benefit. Each is entitled to shape the section touching them before it reaches a room.
2. **A short sponsor statement on the framing.** Specifically: that no current sole-source relationship is being characterised as an error, and that anyone who surfaces a supply risk, a sub-tier surprise, or an ethical finding — including one they should arguably have caught earlier — will be thanked rather than examined. Nothing in this plan works if the first instinct on discovering an unauthorised subcontractor is to not mention it.
3. **A short statement of what is *not* on the table**, agreed in advance: product safety, certification integrity, and the right of any function to stop a shipment. Once those are secure, a surprising amount of the rest becomes discussable.
4. **Publication of findings that are unflattering to us**, including the internal purchasing-practices review in §6.4. That review is the one most likely to be quietly dropped, and the one most likely to change outcomes.

The tone throughout: every function is currently doing what its measures ask of it. The measures are what we can change.

---

## 2. Governance — deliberately light

We would resist standing up a "Supply Chain Risk Function." It would become a reporting layer, and reporting layers absorb the information they are meant to move.

| Role | Holder | Accountability |
|---|---|---|
| **Executive sponsor** | Managing Director | Breaks deadlocks; owns the funding case; signs the code and the no-blame statement |
| **Supply Resilience Lead** (new, single point) | Senior appointment from Procurement or Operations — **selected on evidence of cross-functional credibility, not seniority** | Owns the single risk register, the TTS/TTR position, and the escalation clock |
| **Resilience Cell** | Lead (chair) + Procurement, Operations, Engineering, Quality, Legal/Compliance, Finance — plus, by invitation, whoever actually knows the answer that week | Fortnightly, 45 minutes. Standing agenda: new single points of failure, watchlist movement, open grievances, drill outcomes |
| **Escalation** | Cell → sponsor | Anything unresolved at the second Cell meeting goes up with a one-page written position from each function and is **decided within 5 working days**. Ageing is not a decision |
| **Ethical stop authority** | Compliance lead, unconditional | Authority to suspend a source pending investigation, without Cell majority and without commercial override. Stated in writing |

Two deliberate design choices. First, the Cell has **no fixed membership below the six functions** — it pulls in the buyer, the engineer, the quality inspector who has actually visited the site. Authority in this programme should follow knowledge of the specific supplier, not position. Second, the ethical stop authority is unconditional *because* it makes speed safe to pursue elsewhere. A veto that can be overruled commercially is not a veto; it is a delay.

---

## 3. Diagnostic — Days 0–90

### 3.1 Instruments

| Instrument | Method | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tier-1 census** | Every direct supplier: spend, parts, site address (not HQ), sole/dual status, contract status, tooling ownership, lead time, financial health score | Procurement | Day 30 |
| **Criticality segmentation** | Kraljic-style: supply risk × profit impact. Output: Class A / B / C parts | Resilience Lead | Day 40 |
| **Single-point-of-failure register** | Sole-sourced parts, sole *sites* (two suppliers, one factory), sole sub-tier, sole logistics route, sole port, sole test house, sole certification body | Engineering + Procurement | Day 45 |
| **Time-to-Recover (TTR)** | Per Class A part: realistic days to restore supply from a named alternate — *validated with the supplier, not estimated internally* | Procurement | Day 60 |
| **Time-to-Survive (TTS)** | Days of production sustainable from on-hand + in-transit + WIP before line stop | Operations | Day 60 |
| **Disruption cost reconstruction** | Last 24 months: expedite freight, spot premiums, line stoppages, penalties, lost orders, engineering rework from substitution | Finance | Day 60 |
| **Geographic & geopolitical concentration** | Spend by country, port, and physical cluster (industrial parks, seismic zones, flood plains, water-stressed basins) | Resilience Lead | Day 45 |
| **Ethical salience screen** | Every direct site scored on: country risk, sector risk, migrant-labour intensity, recruitment-agency use, subcontracting likelihood, commodity origin | Compliance | Day 60 |
| **Internal purchasing-practices review** | Our own behaviour: order change frequency, lead-time compression demands, payment performance vs. terms, price-down pressure | Independent reviewer | Day 75 |

### 3.2 The one analytical idea worth adopting from the outset

**Time-to-Survive minus Time-to-Recover.** For each Class A part, the question is not "how likely is a disruption" — a probability we will estimate badly for events we have not imagined — but "if this node vanished on Monday, would we still be building on the day supply returns?"

$$\text{Exposure} = \text{TTR} - \text{TTS}$$

Where the number is positive, we have a gap in days, and we can choose how to close it: buffer stock, a dual source, a design alternate, or a capacity reservation. Where it is negative or zero, **we do nothing** — and that discipline is what stops this programme becoming a generalised inventory build. It also has the useful property of finding the low-value, high-exposure parts that a spend-based analysis will always miss: the £4 connector with an 18-month requalification is a far larger risk than the £40,000 casting with three qualified sources.

### 3.3 Fallback, started Day 0 rather than after disappointment

Sub-tier data will be incomplete — it always is, and suppliers will withhold it for commercial reasons that are entirely legitimate from where they sit. Rather than waiting:

- **Ask for what they will give.** Country of manufacture and site city for the top five inputs, without naming the supplier. This alone locates most cluster risk.
- **Infer the rest.** Trade data, customs records, certification registries (smelter lists, ISO/IATF databases), and — often the fastest route — asking our own engineers, who frequently know exactly where a component actually comes from.
- **Trade access for disclosure.** Longer-term volume commitments, faster payment, or preferred status in exchange for sub-tier transparency. Suppliers will disclose to a customer who is investing in them and will not disclose to one who is benchmarking them.

---

## 4. Segmentation — the decision that governs all others

Not every supplier warrants the same treatment, and pretending otherwise is how these programmes become expensive without becoming safer.

| Segment | Characteristics | Resilience treatment | Ethical treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Strategic** (~5–10% of suppliers, ~50–60% of value) | High risk, high impact; often sole-source, IP-entangled, long qualification | Deep partnership: joint continuity planning, capacity reservation, sub-tier disclosure, executive relationship, open-book where possible | On-site assessment, worker voice, joint remediation plans, capability co-investment |
| **Bottleneck** (low value, high risk) | Small spend, no alternative, long requalification | The buffer-and-alternate segment. Buy time, not volume: stock, design alternates, tooling ownership | Risk-screen; escalate only on salience |
| **Leverage** (high value, low risk) | Competitive markets, substitutable | Multi-source by default; rotate volume; competitive tension | Contractual code + self-assessment + spot verification |
| **Routine** (low value, low risk) | Catalogue, commodity | Consolidate, automate, ignore for resilience purposes | Code acceptance; screen on origin flags only |

**The distribution of effort should be visibly uneven.** If the programme is spending equal attention on routine and strategic suppliers, it has become a compliance exercise.

---

## 5. Resilience architecture

### 5.1 Source strategy — plural, not merely dual

| Instrument | When it fits | Honest cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Dual sourcing (70/30 or 80/20)** | Class A, requalification feasible | 2–8% unit cost premium; qualification cost; volume fragmentation |
| **Dual *site*, single supplier** | Where the relationship is good but geography is concentrated | Cheaper than dual supplier; does not protect against supplier insolvency |
| **Approved alternate, dormant** | Where volume cannot be split economically | Requalification kept warm with an annual token order — *the token order is the point*; a paper alternate is not an alternate |
| **Regional balance ("+1")** | Where a whole country or corridor is the exposure | Landed cost premium 5–20%; offset partially by freight, duty, inventory-in-transit and lead-time reduction |
| **Nearshoring / regionalisation** | High-volume, freight-heavy, demand-volatile | Highest cost, highest lead-time and responsiveness gain; justify per part, never as policy |
| **Capacity reservation with option fee** | Long-lead, high-value, low-frequency | Pay for the right to buy; frequently cheaper than holding the stock |
| **Vertical integration** | Only where the capability is genuinely core and the market has failed | Slow, capital-heavy; a last resort dressed as strategy |

**A caution worth stating.** Dual sourcing is not resilience if both suppliers buy from the same tier-2, sit in the same industrial park, use the same specialist heat-treater, or ship through the same port. Roughly the most common finding in exercises of this kind is that a carefully dual-sourced part has a single point of failure three layers down. The register in §3.1 should be built at the level of **physical site and physical route**, not supplier name.

### 5.2 Design-side resilience — the cheapest lever, and the slowest

Procurement can only choose among the sources engineering has permitted. The largest structural gains are usually here:

- **Part standardisation and rationalisation.** Fewer unique parts, more shared across the range. Reduces qualification burden and increases volume leverage simultaneously.
- **Design for substitution.** Specify to function and performance where possible rather than to a single manufacturer's part number. Where a single part number is genuinely required (certified assemblies, safety-critical items), say so explicitly and accept the buffer cost as the price of the specification.
- **Multi-sourced by design.** A standing rule that new Class A parts require an identified second source *before* design freeze, or a written, signed exception. Exceptions should be granted freely and recorded — the record is what builds the register.
- **Requalification pre-work.** Hold the second-source qualification package at 80% complete: drawings released, supplier identified, quote held

# Lead Time Reduction Plan — Second Draft

**Prepared for review by the Managing Director and the three functional leaders (Production, Quality, Sales), with Engineering and Procurement in attendance.**
*Circulated for comment before any decision is sought. Numbers marked "illustrative" are placeholders to be replaced by the Week 6 business case; the governance, ownership and decision requests are not placeholders and are put forward for approval.*

---

## 0. Executive summary

**The situation, stated plainly but without attribution of fault.** We quote 14 weeks; our fastest competitor quotes 6; Sales reports losing roughly one deal in three on delivery. A previous attempt to compress the schedule produced a warranty spike that took two years to recover from. The three functions currently hold three different, internally coherent explanations of where the time goes. All three may well be partly right, which is precisely why no single function can resolve it.

**The central finding we expect the diagnostic to confirm.** In a build of this type, of a 14-week (≈70 working-day) quoted lead time, we estimate around **55 working days are waiting** — material queues, gate dwell, rework loops, administrative serialisation, and quote padding — and roughly **15 days are genuine value-adding work, of which the certified inspections themselves are about one day.** The prior compression episode, as best we can reconstruct it, compressed the 15 rather than the 55. That is the difference this plan turns on.

**The organising principle.** *Touch time is treated as sacred; queue time is fair game.* Every intervention must pass the test: *does this change what we inspect, or only when and how quickly the part reaches the inspector?* Where an intervention does change a control — and two of them do — it is presented openly as a **substitution of controls with equivalence evidence**, not as a free saving.

**The commitment we would ask colleagues to consider, in two deliberate stages:**

| | Quoted lead time (configure-to-order lane) | Earned by | Target date |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stage 1** | **7 calendar weeks** (35 working days) | Flow, material, gate-dwell and rework improvements demonstrated in a pilot lane | Month 8 |
| **Stage 2** | **6 calendar weeks** (30 working days) | Demonstrated reduction in schedule variance permitting a smaller quote buffer | Month 14–16 |

Sales will understandably prefer to sell the endpoint immediately. It may be worth agreeing together that a **reliable 7 beats an optimistic 6**, and that the buffer is the last thing we spend, not the first.

**Illustrative investment ask (order of magnitude; to be firmed by Week 6):**

| Item | Year-1 cost | Working capital | Note |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Certified sub-assembly stock | — | £2.0–3.0M net | Gross £2.8–4.2M, reduced by aftermarket alignment (§10) |
| Inspection & metrology capacity (3 inspectors + 1 metrology technician) | £0.32M/yr | — | Recruitment lead time 3–6 months; interim third-party source inspection |
| Configurator (quote-to-BOM) | £0.25–0.45M | — | 6–9 months to live; **not** a quick win |
| eQMS / concurrent certification records | £0.30–0.60M | — | 9–12 months; registrar review required |
| In-process metrology, CMM programming, data capture | £0.40–0.70M | — | Phased by gate |
| MRP/ATP configuration | £0.12M | — | |
| Programme resource (lead + analyst) | £0.25M/yr | — | |
| **Total** | **£1.6–2.4M** | **£2.0–3.0M** | |

**Illustrative return.** On assumptions to be validated in Week 2 (200 qualified opportunities/yr, ~£180k average order value, ~37 losses/yr attributed to delivery, recovery of half of those falling in the fast lanes), incremental bookings of **£3.0–3.6M/yr** at ~30% contribution, plus **£0.4–0.7M/yr** of avoided rework, scrap and expedite cost, and a reduction in warranty exposure that we would not attempt to monetise in front of this audience. Indicative payback **20–26 months** including working capital. *If the Week 2 win/loss validation does not support the revenue figure, the correct recommendation is to fund only the near-zero-cost workstreams and stop.*

**Ownership — the change we believe matters most.** Today, end-to-end lead time is nobody's single measure, and each function is being asked to optimise something that makes it worse. We propose a named **Flow Owner** accountable for quoted lead time end-to-end, a weekly **Flow Council**, and a shared scorecard across all three leaders. Details in §2.

**Decisions requested (also listed in §14):** appoint sponsor and Flow Owner (Week 0); authorise the diagnostic and the certification enquiry (Week 0); approve the shared scorecard (Week 4); approve capital and working capital (Week 8, on the business case); approve Stage 1 quoting (Month 8, on pilot evidence).

---

## 1. How we would suggest this plan is taken forward

A plan of this kind will not succeed by being circulated and approved. Before the first Flow Council, we would propose:

1. **Separate one-to-one conversations** with the Production, Quality, Sales, Engineering and Procurement leaders, in seniority order, so that each has the opportunity to shape the parts touching their area *before* anything is presented collectively. Disagreements are far easier to accommodate at that stage than in a room.
2. **A short, sponsor-signed statement on the prior episode** — that it is now understood as a failure of system design under commercial pressure, not of individual judgement; and that **exercising quality stop authority will carry no career consequence, ever, and requires no escalation.** This costs nothing and, in our view, is the precondition for Quality's genuine (rather than formal) participation.
3. **A shared statement of what is not on the table**, agreed in advance: acceptance criteria, gate content, and stop authority. Once colleagues are confident these are secure, a great deal becomes discussable that is currently not.
4. **Publication of every diagnostic finding**, including those unflattering to whichever function commissioned the work, and including any that reflect on management scheduling practice.

The tone throughout should be that all three functions are currently doing what their measures ask of them. The measures are the problem we can change.

---

## 2. Governance, ownership and the alignment question

### 2.1 Structure

| Role | Holder (by position) | Accountability |
|---|---|---|
| **Executive sponsor** | Managing Director | Removes cross-functional deadlocks; signs the no-retribution statement; owns the funding case |
| **Flow Owner** (new, single point of accountability) | Director of Order Fulfilment (or equivalent senior appointment) | **Quoted and actual end-to-end lead time.** Convenes the Council; owns the plan; has release authority over the single sequence (§7D) |
| **Flow Council** | Flow Owner (chair), Production Manager, Quality Director, Sales Director, Engineering Manager, Procurement Manager | Weekly, 60 minutes, standing agenda: tripwire status, gate dwell, kit completeness, lane mix, escalations |
| **Escalation path** | Council → sponsor | Any item unresolved in Council is escalated with a written position from each function and **decided by the sponsor within 48 hours**. Silence is not consent; unresolved items do not simply age |
| **Quality Director** | — | Retains unconditional veto on anything touching gate content, sampling, or certification. This veto is not subject to Council majority |

Placing an explicit veto with Quality is deliberate. It is the mechanism by which speed becomes safe to pursue, and it should be stated in writing rather than assumed.

### 2.2 Shared scorecard — the substantive change

We would propose adding the following to **all three** functional leaders' scorecards, at equal weight, from the next review cycle:

| Measure | Definition |
|---|---|
| **OTIF against the *first* promised date** | Not the revised date. Re-promising is the mechanism by which delay currently becomes invisible |
| **Escape rate** | Defects found downstream of the gate that should have caught them |
| **Quoted-lead-time attainment** | Actual vs. quoted, by lane |

And, more delicately, we would suggest the sponsor consider retiring or neutralising three measures that are, we believe, generating the present friction rather than any individual doing so:

- **Production's utilisation / absorption target.** This measure rewards loading WIP onto the floor, and will quietly resist the WIP cap in §7D. It cannot survive alongside this plan. Suggested replacement: schedule adherence and throughput at the constraint.
- **Quality's inspections-completed throughput measure.** It discourages the very thing we need — inspectors idle at a gate, waiting, so that nothing else waits for them.
- **Sales' commission timing on booked orders regardless of deliverability.** Suggested adjustment: a portion of commission contingent on delivery to the first promised date, which aligns Sales with the lane discipline in §9.

We recognise these are compensation-adjacent matters requiring HR involvement and the sponsor's authority. We would not propose them lightly, but the arithmetic does not work without them.

---

## 3. Diagnostic: Weeks 0–4 (and what to do when the data does not exist)

### 3.1 Instruments

| Instrument | Method | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|---|
| Order-level time ladder | Last 60–100 shipped orders: timestamp every state change from order receipt to ship | Programme analyst | Wk 3 |
| Touch-time vs. elapsed-time ratio | Standard hours ÷ elapsed working hours | Production Manager | Wk 3 |
| **Gate dwell decomposition** | Per gate: *waiting for inspector / inspection / waiting for sign-off / waiting for rework / re-inspection* | Quality Director | Wk 4 |
| Rework loop census | Every NCR: detected where, caused where, days lost, supplier or internal | Quality Director | Wk 4 |
| Material critical-path attribution | Which single line gated each kit? | Procurement Manager | Wk 3 |
| Quote-to-actual variance | By configuration family; exposes padding and whether padding is doing real work | Flow Owner | Wk 3 |
| Configuration Pareto | 24 months of orders clustered by option content | Engineering Manager | Wk 4 |

**Fallback, to be started in Week 0 in parallel rather than after disappointment:** if system timestamps prove absent or unreliable — which is common, and would be nobody's fault — we proceed with (a) manual traveller stamping on the next 20 orders released, (b) a full physical value-stream walk with the three functions present together, and (c) a two-day direct observation study at each certified gate. This yields sufficient resolution in four weeks and avoids eight weeks of data archaeology.

### 3.2 Two validations before any capital is committed

- **Win/loss validation (Owner: Sales Director, with an independent interviewer; due Week 2).** 15–20 structured interviews on lost deals. This is not scepticism toward Sales; lead time is simply the most available and least uncomfortable loss reason in any organisation, and if the true driver is price, reliability or specification, the capital in this plan is misdirected. Sales' credibility is *strengthened*, not exposed, by independent confirmation.
- **Competitor reliability benchmark (Owner: Sales Director; due Week 4).** Does the competitor actually *deliver* in 6 weeks, or quote it? If they routinely miss, then a guaranteed, penalty-backed 7 weeks may be a sharper weapon than an aspirational 6 — and considerably cheaper.

---

## 4. Where the 70 working days go

**Units, stated once and used throughout: all durations in this document are *working days* at 5 per week.** 14 weeks = 70 working days; the 6-week target = 30 working days. Calendar conversions are given in brackets where relevant.

Illustrative decomposition, to be replaced by the diagnostic:

| Segment | Working days | Of which value-adding |
|---|---:|---:|
| Order entry, configuration confirmation, engineering release, contract/credit admin | 7 | 1 |
| Purchasing cycle + longest-lead item wait to kit completion | 19 | 0 |
| Fabrication / machining queue and setup wait | 8 | 3 |
| Assembly | 7 | 5 |
| Certified gate dwell (4 gates) | 7 | 1 |
| Rework and re-inspection loops (probability-weighted) | 5 | 0 |
| Final test, burn-in, certification documentation pack | 6 | 4 |
| Preservation, crating, shipping preparation | 3 | 1 |
| Quote protection buffer | 8 | 0 |
| **Total** | **70 (14 weeks)** | **15** |

| **Leverage** (high value, low risk) | Competitive markets, substitutable | Multi-source by default; rotate volume; competitive tension | Contractual code + self-assessment + spot verification |

### 5.1 Source strategy — plural, not merely dual

| Instrument | When it fits | Honest cost |

## 0. Executive summary

### 0.1 The situation, without attribution of fault

We buy from a supplier base assembled over many years, largely on landed cost and quality performance — which were, at the time, exactly the right criteria, and were applied well. Recent events have made visible a second and third set of criteria that were always present but rarely priced:

- *How quickly could this source be replaced, if it stopped?*
- *What is happening two tiers behind it that we cannot currently see?*

Both questions are now being put to us by customers, by insurers, by lenders, and — increasingly, and with legal force — by regulators in the markets we sell into. Several of them are asked in tender questionnaires that we currently answer with goodwill rather than evidence.

### 0.2 The two agendas are usually presented as a trade-off. We would gently suggest they are largely one programme

The same blind spot — no visibility below tier 1 — produces both the sudden allocation shock and the unauthorised subcontracting to an unassessed site. The same commercial reflex — squeeze price, compress lead time, change the order late — produces both the financially fragile supplier and the excessive-overtime finding. A programme that treats resilience and responsible sourcing as one *visibility-and-relationship* problem will cost materially less than two programmes that treat them as separate compliance functions.

That said, we would not want to overstate the overlap in front of this audience, because two things do **not** overlap:

1. **Severity is measured differently.** Resilience exposure is measured in days and pounds to us. Human-rights salience is measured in harm to people, and a £4,000-a-year supplier can carry the most severe finding in the book. The two prioritisation lists will therefore differ, and §4.3 states plainly where they part company.
2. **Exit is not symmetrical.** Resilience wants a second source so we can walk away. Responsible sourcing usually asks us *not* to walk away, because abrupt withdrawal transfers the harm to the workers concerned. §6.7 addresses this directly.

### 0.3 The organising principle we would put forward

> *We do not buy parts. We buy the continued ability of a specific site, with specific people, to make them.*
>
> Everything that follows attempts to make that ability **visible**, **replaceable**, and **worth preserving** — in that order.

### 0.4 What we would ask colleagues to consider committing to, in three deliberate stages

|---|---|---|---|

(b) **Targeted high-enforcement input screen** (forced-labour import bans; sanctions/denied-party) on any exposure to polysilicon, aluminium, cotton, certain downstream metals and their derivatives | Legal/Compliance + Procurement, using existing data; near-zero capital | **Day 30** |
| **Stage 1** | Every Tier-1 **site** mapped; every single point of failure named and owned; salience screen across 100% of direct spend; grievance route live at the highest-salience sites | Diagnostic + existing data; near-zero capital | **Day 90** |

| **Stage 3** | Sub-tier traceability to the standard of legal defensibility for those obligations Stage 0 confirms apply to us; disruption drills *passed*, not merely run | Multi-tier mapping, chain-of-custody, supplier development | **Month 24–36** |

The first draft placed sub-tier traceability entirely in Stage 3. On reflection that was a sequencing error we would rather correct now than defend later: goods-detention risk is present tense, not a Month-24 concern.
